title: Ember and Rogation days
hookLine: old seasonal fasting days to bless the harvest and the fields

lines: A WHOLE PARISH ON A WALK.
cards: In English villages, there was once a spring day when the whole parish went for a walk.
The priest led the way with a cross, the choir sang, and the people followed the edge of the parish, field by field, stopping at boundary stones and old trees to pray for the crops.
Children were sometimes bumped against the markers so they'd remember where the line was.
It was called beating the bounds, and it belonged with a set of old fasting and praying days that are easy to miss on today's calendar.

teach.b: First, the Ember days. Four times a year, near the turn of each season, the Church kept three days of fasting and prayer: a Wednesday, a Friday and a Saturday.
Their Latin name was quattuor tempora, the four times: in Advent, in Lent, after Pentecost, and in September after the feast of the Holy Cross.
They were very old, and some historians think they grew from Rome's own seasons of harvest, vintage and sowing.
They gave thanks for each season and asked a blessing on the next, and Ember Saturdays became the traditional days for ordinations.
Then the Rogation days, from the Latin rogare, to ask.

Tradition says that around 470, in Vienne in Gaul, after fires, earthquakes and wild animals had terrified the town, Bishop Mamertus called three days of fasting and processions before Ascension Thursday.
The custom spread, and Rogation processions through the fields, asking God to bless the planting, became part of village life in many lands.
Since the calendar reform of 1969, both are left to each country's bishops, and where they aren't kept, they've faded. But the instinct behind them is as old as the Psalms.

teach.h: THE EARTH HATH YIELDED HER FRUIT.
teach.b: As one psalm puts it, in the Douay-Rheims: "The earth hath yielded her fruit." Food doesn't start in the store. It starts in soil, weather and somebody's work, and these days were the Church remembering that out loud.

how: Since 1969, Ember and Rogation days are set by each bishops' conference and are little kept in many places; some parishes, especially rural ones, still hold Rogation processions to bless fields and gardens in spring, and some Catholics keep the Ember days as voluntary days of fasting.

games.q: it's around 470 in Vienne. fires and earthquakes have terrified the town. you're Bishop Mamertus. what do you do?
o: tell everyone to leave the town.
call three days of fasting and processions before Ascension.
wait for the emperor to send help.
games.why: tradition says he called three days of fasting and processions. the Rogation days spread from there across Europe.

practice: Pick up something you'll eat today, an apple, a slice of bread, a handful of rice, or picture your last meal, and trace it backward: the store, the truck, the warehouse, the farm, the field, the rain, the hands that picked it.
Stay with each step for a breath. If you pray, ask God to bless the fields and the people who work them; if you don't, simply be grateful, step by step.
